name: Agnes Samuel
social_status: Village woman, Warboys, Huntingdonshire; daughter of Alice and John Samuel
biography:
Agnes Samuel was the daughter of Alice and John Samuel of Warboys, all three executed together for witchcraft at Huntingdon on April 7, 1593 — one of the only three-generation family executions in English witch trial history. Agnes's involvement in the case developed as the prosecution of her parents expanded to implicate the entire household. The accusation logic that drove English witch prosecution frequently extended through family networks, and Agnes, living in the same household as her parents, was identified as a participant in the alleged diabolical conspiracy.

Agnes Samuel confessed to her role in the bewitchment of the Throckmorton children alongside her parents. The confession, like those of her parents, was almost certainly produced through sustained social pressure rather than formal torture, as the English legal tradition did not employ judicial torture as readily as continental jurisdictions. The Throckmorton family's sustained engagement with the Samuel household across four years of accusation created conditions of extreme social pressure that were capable of producing confession without formal torture.

Her execution alongside her father and mother makes the Warboys case unique in English prosecution history for the totality of a family's destruction. The three were hanged at Huntingdon, and their estate was used to endow the anti-witchcraft sermon at Queens' College, Cambridge. Agnes Samuel appears as the youngest of the condemned, and her execution raises the question historians have often posed about the transmission of belief and practice within accused families.
arrest_narrative: Agnes was arrested as part of the prosecution of the entire Samuel household in the Warboys case. She was accused of participation in her parents' alleged witchcraft conspiracy and was tried alongside them.

interrogation_and_confession.final_confession_summary: Confessed to participation in family witchcraft against the Throckmorton children; specific confession content less fully documented than her mother Alice's

accusations_against_them: Maleficium as part of household conspiracy with parents
historiographical_significance: Agnes Samuel's execution as part of the three-generation Warboys family hanging makes the case exceptional in English witch prosecution history. The family execution illustrates how accusation networks expanded through household and kinship ties, and raises questions historians have explored about whether shared domestic space created shared risk, or whether accusers found it easier to implicate entire families once the primary accused was identified.
source_method: The Most Strange and Admirable Discovery of the Three Witches of Warboys (1593 pamphlet); Huntingdonshire assize records; analyzed in Macfarlane's Witchcraft in Tudor and Stuart England (1970) and Levack
